The three diagrams that carry it project onto two Lorentz structures: the tree-level one, which rescales the rate, and that of the CP-even anomalous coupling $b_Z$, which changes the polarization of the final-state $Z$ boson. To assess how well quantum state tomography constrains the $hZZ$ anomalous couplings and the trilinear coupling at FCC-ee, we compute the helicity density matrix of the $Z$ boson, for an effective vertex that also includes a CP-odd anomalous coupling $\tilde b_Z$, together with its complete one-loop correction in the Standard Model. With these corrections and no other new physics in the effective vertex, quantum state tomography determines $κ_λ$ to $\pm 3.9$, or $\pm 2.9$ with the full angular information, independently of the rate and of the normalization of the vertex, and not far from the limit $δκ_λ\simeq 1$ set by the quantum Fisher information. Without assumptions on the new physics, quantum tomography directly bounds the anomalous couplings at the $10^{-3}$ level, improving on the existing projections. The density matrix also characterizes the $Z$ boson as a qutrit. At $365$ GeV its state in the central region is pure enough to violate the Klyachko--Can--Binicioğlu--Shumovsky contextuality inequality, $\mathbb{CNTXT}_5 = 2.06$ at $θ= π/2$ against the non-contextual bound $2$. We also quantify the purity and the amount of magic of the $Z$ boson state, using the mana, the stabilizer Rényi entropy and the robustness of magic for the latter. At fixed angle, purity, contextuality and magic are robust against anomalous couplings of the size probed by the tomography. The inclusive state, instead, is neither contextual in this test nor magic in the helicity basis.

papers.title: Quantum Preparation without Disturbance: Information Costs and Hypothesis Testing
papers.abstract: We determine the minimum information cost of preparing either of two quantum states with one common device while preserving its memory. Measured by the Umegaki relative entropy between the two possible memory states, this minimum is the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy of the target states. If the memory may instead be consumed, the minimum is their Umegaki relative entropy. More generally, for any divergence satisfying data processing, memory preservation selects the maximal extension of its classical restriction. We also study the cost of requiring only finitely many outputs, with the costs increasing from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy as the number of outputs grows. Finally, we consider hypothesis testing of an unknown device over independent runs. The optimal Stein exponent per run converges to the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy whenever the number of outputs per run diverges. This gives an operational characterization of the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy in quantum statistics.

papers.title: On the Construction of New Families of Distance Equienergetic Graphs
papers.abstract: For a graph $G$ with vertex set $V(G)=\{v_{i}:1\leq i \leq p\}$ and edge set $E(G)=\{e_{j}:1\leq j \leq q\},$ its subdivision graph $S_G$ is generalized to $S_{G}(n,m),$ by replacing each vertex $v_{i}$ with $n$ vertices and each edge-vertex $e_{j}$ with $m$ vertices, with each copy having the same neighbors as the vertex it replaces. Building on this construction, we define the generalized subdivision vertex join $S_{G_{1}}(n,m)\dot{\vee} G_{2}$ and the generalized subdivision edge join $S_{G}(n,m)\veebar G_{2},$ which extend the known subdivision vertex and subdivision edge join of graphs. In this paper, we determine the distance spectrum of $S_{G_{1}}(n,n)\dot{\vee} G_{2}$ and $S_{G}(n,n)\veebar G_{2},$ when $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ are regular graphs. As an application, we construct new families of $D$-cospectral graphs and $D$-equienergetic graphs of diameter $4.$

papers.title: Forget the Lineage: Forward-Secure, Lineage-Complete Cryptographic Erasure for LLM-Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents keep a long-term memory that the model itself writes: summaries, extracted facts and embeddings derived from what users said. Deleting a message is therefore not enough: its derivatives, storage residue and backups survive. We define lineage-complete forward-secure erasure: after a forget request, an adversary that later obtains all storage and the agent's current keys learns nothing about the forgotten input or any memory derived from it. We present LinEra, which encrypts each memory under a key derived from its parents' keys along the derivation graph; source keys come from a puncturable pseudorandom function, so forgetting is a single puncture and every descendant becomes unreadable without being located. A sound lineage rule records as parents everything the writer saw, which confines all influence of a source to its descendants. We prove security and lineage integrity and integrate LinEra with mem0. With real LLMs from two families (1.5B to 7B parameters) writing the memory of LoCoMo conversations, an attacker holding every file and the current keys recovers, on all ten conversations written by the largest model, 70 of 71 forgotten secrets after logical deletion, 67 with per-object or epoch keys, and none with LinEra; the same holds for every writer tested. The price is a larger forgetting radius, which follows a simple law in the writer's fan-in: forgetting 1% of turns erases 73.0% of derived memories with session-level summaries but only 3.8% with four-turn windows, which also answer better; re-deriving restores what is lost.

papers.title: Parameterized Weakest-Precondition Calculus for Fine-grained Properties of Quantum Loops
papers.abstract: Quantum loops may execute arbitrarily many iterations, and understanding their runtime behavior requires knowing how often they terminate, how long terminating runs take, and how common very long runs are. We develop a compositional weakest-precondition framework for analyzing these properties on possibly infinite-dimensional state spaces. It uses parameterized predicates: families of quantum effects indexed by a positive observation scale. These families retain runtime information even when the expected runtime is infinite and can be reused through sequential composition and nested loops. We prove that weakest-precondition equations for loops have unique solutions in the parameterized predicate domain. From the asymptotic behavior of the derived weakest preconditions, we then recover these runtime properties and quantify the influence of very long terminating executions. For the classic discrete-time quantum walk on the one-dimensional infinite line with one absorbing boundary at the origin and the Hadamard gate as its coin operator, we verify its termination probability $2/π$, conditional mean $π/2$, and logarithmic growth of the conditional capped second moment. We then reuse the walk's specification to verify the termination probability and conditional mean runtime of an outer loop that repeatedly invokes it.

papers.title: Experimental characterization of magnetic multipole fields up to octupole order using smartphone magnetometry
papers.abstract: The multipole expansion is one of the organising ideas of electromagnetism: far from a localised source the field is dominated by its lowest non-vanishing moment, and each successive order decays one power of the distance faster. Although the dipole field is routinely measured in introductory laboratories, higher orders are seldom explored experimentally, because the fields are weak, decay very rapidly and require careful positioning. Here we show that with four identical neodymium cube magnets, a sheet of graph paper and the magnetometer of a smartphone, first-year students can build and characterise not one but three distinct magnetic octupoles (linear, planar and `square' arrangements), together with the dipole and the two quadrupoles that serve as reference. A simple notation and a compact set of formulae, based on the spatial Cartesian moments $M_{pq}=\sum_k m_k x_k^p z_k^q$ of the array, predict which field component survives at each measuring position and how it decays. The measured exponents are $n\simeq 3$, $4$ and $5$ for dipole, quadrupole and octupole arrangements, and the measured prefactors show fair quantitative consistency with the independently determined dipole moment of the magnets once nominal geometry and spacer effects are taken into account. We discuss the systematic effects that limit the octupole measurements (higher-order terms at short distance, residual lower-order moments at long distance, the location of the sensor inside the phone) and the ways in which the activity can be extended. The experiment generalises and unifies previous smartphone-based measurements of dipoles, linear quadrupoles and a linear octupole.

papers.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.

papers.title: The minimal excludant of $\ell$-regular overpartitions
papers.abstract: Andrews and Newman \cite{AN1} introduced the minimal excludant (mex) of an integer partition, and Aricheta and Donato \cite{AD} extended it to overpartitions. More recently, Meher \cite{Meher} and Tejash, Bhowmick and Meher \cite{TBM} studied the analogous statistic for $\ell$-regular partitions. In this article, for an integer $\ell\ge 2$, we define the minimal excludant $\omex_\ell(π)$ of an $\ell$-regular overpartition $π$ as the smallest positive integer that is not divisible by $\ell$ and does not occur as a non-overlined part of $π$. We study $\sm{\ell}(n)$, the sum of $\omex_\ell(π)$ over all $\ell$-regular overpartitions $π$ of $n$. We obtain generating functions for $\sm{\ell}(n)$ as eta-quotients for $\ell=2$ and $\ell=3$. Later, motivated from \cite{TBM}, we obtained explicit generating functions for $\sm{\ell}(n)$. We show that $\sm{\ell}(n)$ is weakly increasing in $n$, and we derive Hardy--Ramanujan type asymptotic formulas for $\sm{2}(n)$ and $\sm{3}(n)$. We then determine the parity of both functions completely: $\sm{2}(n)$ is even for every $n\ge 1$, while $\sm{3}(n)$ is odd if and only if $n=0$ or $n$ is a centred hexagonal number. Also, we obtain for every $\ell\ge3$, $\sm{\ell}(n)$ is odd for infinitely many $n$, and the number of such $n\le X$ is $\gg\sqrt{X}$. Finally, we establish congruences for these functions modulo $3$, $4$ and $8$.

papers.title: Cross-Fitted Doubly Robust Estimation with Student-t Outcome Engines: ECM Algorithms, Monte Carlo Evidence and Schistosomiasis Programme Data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
papers.abstract: Routine data on preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis are confounded, clustered, heavy-tailed and heaped. We study how cross-fitted augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimators behave, and how they should be computed, when least squares is replaced by Student-t outcome engines: Huber and t iteratively reweighted least squares, and a two-component t scale-mixture regression fitted by an ECM algorithm, alongside a residual-clipped augmentation. We give four short propositions (exact AIPW bias, the efficiency bound, the estimand of clipping, monotone ascent of a scale-constrained ECM), a single-file Python implementation with cluster-level cross-fitting, cluster-robust standard errors and a cluster bootstrap, and a Monte Carlo study with up to 1000 replications per cell. Robust outcome engines leave AIPW unchanged (RMSE differences at most 0.002), whereas clipping cuts RMSE by 26-45% under symmetric contamination, under-covers, and, as a plasmode experiment built on real covariates and residuals shows, shifts the estimand when residual laws differ between arms. One-sided artefacts that differ between arms bias every estimator. Heaped data also break naive code: the MAD scale collapses and the mixture likelihood is unbounded, and we give simple guards. Applied to 1485 rounds in 362 health zones of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (ESPEN, 2014-2025), integrated delivery appears to raise programme coverage by 17.4 percentage points, yet epidemiological coverage differs by only 0.9: the gap comes from targeting denominators, a real differential artefact that no outcome engine can remove.

papers.title: PRISM: A Post-Prediction Reliability Framework for Evidence-Guided Correction and Selective Abstention
papers.abstract: A model may produce a prediction with high confidence and still get the outcome wrong. This is a challenge in sequential applications, where the system evolves over time and deployment data may differ from the data used during training. To address this issue, we propose PRISM (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism), a framework that evaluates prediction reliability after the initial output is generated. It estimates the risk of error and examines predictions identified as potentially unreliable. For these cases, PRISM analyses available signals, retrieves similar situations from historical data, and verifies whether an alternative prediction is supported by the evidence. It can then retain the original prediction, apply a verified correction, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate PRISM on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Ball-by-ball records are converted into over-level observations to capture changes in match conditions throughout an innings. To preserve temporal order, earlier IPL seasons are used for training, IPL 2024 for validation, and IPL 2025-2026 for out-of-time testing. The dataset contains 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches, with the test partition comprising 2,568 observations from 142 matches. In one experimental record, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and HistGradientBoosting achieve accuracies of 65.2%, 68.4%, and 70.2%, respectively. The corresponding PRISM evaluation reports a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.

papers.title: Hello Again: Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters to Brute-Force Windows Hello PINs
papers.abstract: Windows Hello is the primary authentication mechanism on over one billion Windows 11 devices, supporting PINs as short as four digits. Such low-entropy PINs are viable only because the TPM's anti-hammering protection mitigates brute-force attacks. Most modern x86 platforms rely on firmware TPMs (fTPMs) that persist their non-volatile (NV) state, including the lockout state, to SPI flash. On newer platforms, rollback prevention of this state is delegated to the flash chip via Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMCs), a JEDEC-standardized mechanism operating over a physically accessible bus. We present the first practical security analysis of RPMC in shipping x86 systems. Using low-cost interposer hardware, we identify multiple implementation flaws, two of which fundamentally undermine RPMC's security model: First, Winbond SPI flash - the leading NOR flash vendor with over 25% market share - leaks its HMAC key under voltage glitching, enabling arbitrary counter forgery. Second, AMD's NV controller does not verify RPMC increments, so an interposer can suppress them unnoticed. Moreover, AMD platforms without RPMC flash appear to lack NV rollback protection altogether: on two AMD desktops, reflashing an old image resets the fTPM's lockout counters. Both flaws enable rollbacks of the fTPM's NV state (AMD, Intel, or Pluton), including its lockout counters. We demonstrate this end-to-end on locked, encrypted hardware: our setup finds a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN in 40 hours instead of 69 days. A compromised PIN also grants access to device-bound keys and Hello-based enterprise SSO. The same primitive defeats BitLocker's TPM+PIN pre-boot protector, reducing the worst-case time for a default-length 6-digit PIN from 19 years to 20 days.

papers.title: Efficient Poincaré Convolutions through Patch-Statistics Factorization
papers.abstract: Published implementations of the Poincaré convolution in Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ (HNN++) map every overlapping image patch to the Poincaré ball before evaluating its score. We show that the clipped score depends on each patch only through two statistics, its squared norm and its inner products with the filters, which a native convolution and a single-channel box filter compute directly. The factorized layer therefore evaluates the specified score exactly, without constructing ball-valued patches, and its single-precision outputs and gradients agree with double-precision evaluations at least as closely as those of the explicit reference. On an RTX A6000 under two versions of JAX, complete training updates of a Poincaré U-Net and a Poincaré ResNet-20 are 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than the faster of two explicit implementations that map patches to the ball (1.2 to 1.4 times against an explicit implementation that skips this mapping); on a V100, the gain over the gather-based one persists as the ResNet-20 is widened eightfold. In 15 paired training runs per task, updates are 2.0 and 1.8 times faster than a reference that follows the published execution order, with no consistent change in final segmentation or classification quality, and peak memory falls by 38 to 55% in a U-Net scaling study. Replacing the convolutions of the official PyTorch Hyperbolic U-Net makes its training step 1.4 times faster with half the memory. Evaluating an existing layer from its patch statistics thus makes Poincaré convolutional networks cheaper to train in the tested models and software stacks.

papers.title: Muon Attains $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ Iteration Complexity under Shuffling
papers.abstract: Muon is a stochastic first-order optimizer for matrix-valued parameters. It maintains an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients in a momentum buffer with coefficient $β$, and orthogonalizes the buffer to obtain the update direction. Muon has been reported to accelerate and stabilize the training of large language models. In practice, it is often used with shuffling (sampling without replacement), where each epoch visits the components of a finite-sum objective in a permuted order. However, its iteration complexity in this setting remains open. We analyze Muon under shuffling, with the momentum buffer orthogonalized by the polar map. For smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ iteration complexity for finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point. This guarantee holds for every sequence of permutations, covering random reshuffling, shuffle once, and the incremental gradient method. This complexity matches that of stochastic gradient descent under shuffling in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, and improves on Muon's $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ complexity under sampling with replacement. Our guarantee requires a problem-dependent $β$ that approaches one as the number of components grows. In contrast, no fixed $β$ guarantees convergence to stationarity for every number of components. We show this by constructing a family of smooth convex problems on which, for any fixed $β\in[0,1)$, Muon remains bounded away from stationarity once the number of components is sufficiently large. This failure occurs for every sequence of permutations and persists even with small stepsizes. These results suggest two practical tuning rules: if the training loss stops decreasing even after reducing the stepsize, increase $β$; when increasing $β$, reduce the stepsize accordingly.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Models as Spatial Priors for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.

papers.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
papers.abstract: Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

papers.title: Optimizing Drilling Trajectories in Multi-Material Structures Using Quantum Annealers
papers.abstract: In this work we present a quantum-hybrid optimization approach for planning drilling trajectories on multi-material structures, with the objective of minimizing total energy consumption. The proposed formulation models the drilling process as a constrained routing problem in which each hole must be visited while accounting for heterogeneous material properties, material-dependent drilling costs and displacement energy, as well as tool-wear penalties. Our method incorporates realistic industrial constraints, including open-path routing and mandatory grouping of holes belonging to the same material to avoid frequent tool-bit changes. The modeled problem is solved using D-Wave's Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver. To evaluate performance, we benchmark instances ranging from 10 to 55 holes with varying material distributions and cost matrices. The results highlight the capability of quantum-hybrid optimization to handle complex multi-physics constraints and to generate energy-efficient drilling sequences under realistic manufacturing conditions.

papers.title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
papers.abstract: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.

papers.title: Query Processing with eBPF-Offload on Computational Storage
papers.abstract: The idea of pushing computation to storage devices has been explored for decades. In recent years, research has focused on computational storage, i.e., devices that allow a host to execute functions as I/O commands on local data. Today, the NVMe and SNIA computational storage standards share an execution model in which the host invokes functions on the device, on data that the host has moved into device memory. Both standards single out eBPF as a format for functions offloaded by the host. In this paper, we study whether this form of computational storage is a good match for query processing. We present the design and implementation of Delilah, a prototype based on an open-hardware device that implements the standard execution model on an actual device and runs eBPF programs calling device-resident functions. As an initial step, we hand-coded a portion of SSB Q3.3 for execution on the device, aiming to integrate computational storage with a database system's storage manager. The series of experiments that we ran showed that offloading gains little over host execution, execution degenerates into column-at-a-time processing, and time is spent staging and moving data in device memory. Because these roadblocks stem from the execution model rather than from the query, we did not pursue integration further. We detail these limitations and lay the groundwork for a different computational storage model better aligned with data-intensive workloads.

papers.title: Mirror symmetry of $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$ boundary conditions with Nahm poles
papers.abstract: We propose mirror symmetry between $\mathcal{N}=(0,4)$ boundary conditions with Nahm poles and Neumann boundary conditions with boundary Fermi multiplets in 3d $\mathcal{N}=4$ non-Abelian gauge theories, including $U(N)$ SQCD, $T[SU(N)]$ and the ADHM theories. We obtain the half-indices of the Nahm pole boundary conditions from those of the Dirichlet boundary conditions by Higgsing, where the boundary fugacities are specialized along the principal embedding of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. We check that they agree with the half-indices of the dual Neumann boundary conditions. In the twist limits they give closed-form formulas for the vacuum characters of the boundary vertex operator algebras of Costello and Gaiotto. We find that the unflavored vacuum characters are eta-quotients times quasimodular forms, which we write explicitly in terms of Eisenstein series for all our examples.

papers.title: Quasinormal modes of dyonic axion black holes with nonlinear electrodynamics
papers.abstract: We study quasinormal modes (QNMs) of static charged black holes with a massless axion and nonlinear electrodynamics (NED). Without NED corrections, we compute the complex QNM frequencies of five oscillatory mode families in the system of five dynamical degrees of freedom. These families are continued from the fundamental Reissner--Nordström (RN) modes. Axion coupling generically breaks gravitational and electromagnetic parity isospectrality. At representative nonzero couplings, all five frequencies are distinct even on purely electric RN backgrounds without axion hair. Adding magnetic charge sources axion hair, couples all five perturbations, and modifies their oscillation frequencies and damping rates. Additional purely imaginary growing modes occur in some strong-coupling benchmarks. The known electromagnetic--scalar spectral degeneracy at $Q/M=\sqrt{7}/4$ for $\ell=2$ in the decoupled RN limit explains the linear frequency splitting induced by a small axion coupling. We include two quartic NED interactions obtained by squaring the two standard electromagnetic invariants. With the axion decoupled and equal quartic coefficients, electromagnetic duality makes the first-order NED frequency shift of each individual gravitational or electromagnetic branch independent of electric--magnetic charge composition at fixed $Q/M$. For unequal coefficients, duality instead constrains the sum of the first-order NED frequency shifts within each isolated RN parity pair. Depending on the coefficients, NED increases or decreases the damping rates by about one percent in representative backgrounds, while the quartic terms remain small compared with the local Maxwell energy density throughout the exterior. The QNM frequencies and NED shifts obtained with the spectral method agree with independent integration-and-matching results at representative parameter values.

papers.title: Positive Weights Do Not Certify TWFE Inference: A Design Diagnostic under Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. Under a local treatment-effect drift, the statistic for the equally weighted treated-cell effect has worst-case mean shift $(c/q)Γ$, where $Γ=\sqrt{N_1}\|w-u\|_2$ is design-only and $q$ is the cluster-score noise scale. Projection matches the exposure to cohort, event-time, additive, and saturated group-time pilots; when residualized treatment is constant within treated group-time cells, $Γ_{\mathrm{gt}}=Γ$. A direct score estimator is feasible with fixed panel length as clusters grow. Because a debiased quadratic pilot is nonregular at zero, we use two regular one-sided procedures: a reverse-triangle multiplier lower bound to detect unsafe envelopes and covariance-aware noncentral-$χ^2$ inversion to certify adequacy. At $5\%$ nominal size with a five-point tolerance, the shift threshold is $0.652$. In the Callaway--Sant'Anna minimum-wage panel, where every treated-cell weight is positive, the saturated $95\%$ lower shift bound is $0.793$, so conventional inference is not uniformly certified. A complementary Brazilian property-tax reanalysis with $2{,}840$ municipalities withholds certification in all four classes; its smallest lower bound is $1.040$. Under the maintained many-cluster approximation, castle-doctrine homicide passes for additive cohort-plus-event-time heterogeneity with a $95\%$ upper bound of $0.236$; its saturated covariance lacks one required rank. Divorce is inconclusive. These envelopes are not predictions of realized rejection. The diagnostic separates point correction, uniform exposure, and statistically warranted certification.

papers.title: COPASI Skills: Agent Skills for COPASI analyses through Basico
papers.abstract: Biochemical models represent biological systems as networks of reactions that describe the production, consumption, and transformation of molecular species over time. These models provide a quantitative framework for analyzing system dynamics and enable computational experiments that complement traditional wet-lab approaches, helping researchers gain mechanistic insight and make predictive assessments of biological behavior. COPASI is a widely used program for simulating and analyzing those models. These tasks are made availabe to Python through Basico. COPASI Skills is a set of instruction files that tell an assistant how to drive Basico for one analysis at a time. Each skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file. A short description at the top tells the assistant when the skill applies, and the rest of the file states which calls to make, which files to write, and which potential neighboring skill to choose additionally. A researcher can ask for example, in ordinary language, for a time course, a fit, or a published model. The assistant follows the matching skill and leaves tables or a report next to the model. The collection is released under a two-clause BSD license from [https://github.com/fbergmann/copasi-skills](https://github.com/fbergmann/copasi-skills).

papers.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.

papers.title: Folding Language Models into Themselves
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.

papers.title: Any Channel Count, One Token Stream: Incorporating Spatial Audio Understanding and Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio phase relations encode source locations, yet existing large audio-language models (LALM) reduce audio to single-channel content to stabilise general audio understanding, leaving spatial information for direction, distance, and source-relation questions unused. We present SpheraAudio, which accepts recordings with any channel count -- mono, stereo, First-Order Ambisonics (FOA), or higher -- and maps them into a single token stream. A spatial encoder turns complex multichannel spectra into spatial tokens interleaved with audio tokens at corresponding temporal positions. Spatial Multimodal RoPE (SMRoPE) makes each token's modality identity and temporal slot visible to rotary attention without altering the language model's original RoPE. Training runs in three stages -- spatial-encoder pretraining, projector alignment, and joint supervised-and-reinforcement learning -- progressing from geometric supervision to language-based spatial decisions, with answers trained as explicit spatial chain-of-thought: step-by-step geometric reasoning over the heard scene. Current benchmarks tie questions to a fixed channel-count format and score answers without spatial reasoning evidence. We introduce SpheraQA, which spans mono, stereo, and FOA recordings and organises questions hierarchically from single-attribute perception through cross-source relations to multi-step reasoning, scored programmatically against simulated scene geometry and real-recording annotations with step-by-step solution references. Across SpheraQA and public spatial-audio benchmarks, SpheraAudio sets a new performance standard for spatial audio understanding. It supports high-precision localisation, tracking, and reasoning over static and moving sound sources while preserving strong general-audio capabilities. We will release code, SpheraQA, and evaluation metrics to support reproducibility.

papers.title: Multi-GPU Tridiagonal Partition Algorithm
papers.abstract: This paper presents a multi-GPU version and a multi-GPU recursive version of the parallel partition method for systems of linear algebraic equations with tridiagonal coefficient matrices and their implementations in CUDA. Computational experiments on one and two GPU cards, for different system sizes and with different number of recursive steps are conducted. The results are analyzed and discussed.

papers.title: PoliMop: Policy-in-the-Loop Motion Planning in 3D Spaces for Mobile Robots
papers.abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.

papers.title: Pressure dependent DFT study of mechanical, thermal, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of EuCd2As2: a magnetic semimetal
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the pressure-dependent physical properties of EuCd2As2, a magnetically and topologically rich compound with potential applications in spintronics and optoelectronics technologies. We have investigated the structural, mechanical, thermophysical, acoustic, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of this material at pressures of 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 GPa. The calculated lattice parameters at zero pressure are in good agreement with experimental values. The mechanical stability of EuCd2As2 is maintained over the investigated pressure range. The elastic constants, bulk modulus, shear modulus, and Young's modulus are found to be tunable with applied pressure. The compound undergoes a brittle to ductile transition at higher pressures. The Debye temperature, melting temperature, and Grüneisen parameter are found to be strongly pressure-dependent. Phonon thermal conductivity has been evaluated. The electronic properties of EuCd2As2 were studied through band structure and density of states (DOS). The effect of pressure up to 8 GPa was investigated for the ferromagnetic (FM) phase. At 0 GPa, the calculated FM band structure exhibits no band gap at the Fermi level, which confirms the semimetallic nature of EuCd2As2. The net magnetic moment of 6.96 μ_B per unit cell was obtained for this compound indicating its potential for spintronics application. The optical properties, including the dielectric function, refractive index, absorption coefficient, optical conductivity, reflectivity, and loss function, are calculated. The calculated optical spectra indicate strong absorption in the visible and ultraviolet regions, suggesting that EuCd2As2 may have potential for optoelectronic applications.

papers.title: Modular Structure of the ADHM Effective Twisted Superpotential
papers.abstract: The Cardy limit of M2-brane indices retains nonperturbative information through the effective twisted superpotential, including corrections exponentially suppressed at large rank. We investigate the flavor dependence of these corrections in the three-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ $\mathrm U(N)$ ADHM theory at the universal twist. For $N_f=1,2,4$ fundamental hypermultiplets, we conjecture that the full exponential remainder of the selected Bethe critical value is an absolutely convergent divisor sum obtained by applying a first-order differential operator to an Eichler integral of a weight-four Eisenstein form. Resolving this remainder requires the additive constant, which we evaluate from its known integral representation as finite Clausen sums for every positive integer $N_f$. Expanding the integral together with the shifted-rank power determines the type-IIA coefficients of the perturbative contribution at arbitrary genus and their factorial growth. With this subtraction fixed, the proposed sums reproduce independently computed Bethe critical values at up to $800$-digit accuracy, including low ranks that test the continuation beyond the reconstructed sectors. The flavor-one expression agrees with level-one ABJM, whereas the two- and four-flavor completions have distinct divisor laws related by exact dissection identities to finite combinations of ABJM functions. The comparison supports a shared weight-four organization of nonperturbative Bethe data beyond the mirror pair, with arithmetic that distinguishes the theories. Through the finite-rank Cardy relation, the proposed completion predicts the entire $1/ω$ coefficient of the selected vacuum contribution to the superconformal index, retaining these theory-dependent corrections in its leading exponent.

papers.title: Model Choice or Model Bias? How stellar spectral libraries and activity modelling choices influence Ariel spectra- I. Forward model
papers.abstract: The Ariel mission will conduct a population-level survey of approximately 1000 exoplanet atmospheres across its nominal lifetime, requiring unprecedented consistency in the treatment of stellar contamination of transmission spectra. We present a systematic comparison of stellar spectral libraries and modelling approaches for computing facular and spot contamination spectra across the full Ariel wavelength range (0.5-7.8 microns) for six stellar spectral types spanning F3 to M2. Using a surface resolved forward model with approximately 200 randomly generated active region configurations per spectral type, we compute contamination spectra at Ariel Tier 3 resolution and compare three 1D spectral libraries against 3D MHD stellar atmosphere spectra as a physical ground truth. We find that library-dependent differences in the facular treatment introduce systematic biases exceeding the Ariel Tier 3 sensitivity threshold of approximately 20 ppm across most of the wavelength range, for most spectral types and activity levels considered. These biases align with the absorption bands of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane, rendering them indistinguishable from genuine atmospheric signals at Ariel's precision. Our results demonstrate hat the choice of stellar spectral library, in particular the faculae treatment is a critical and currently underappreciated source of systematic error for Ariel atmospheric characterisation. The impact on atmospheric retrievals is quantified in a companion paper.

papers.title: On the spectrality of non-homogeneous self-similar measures
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-cylinder difference-set obstruction to the existence of an exponential orthonormal basis for a compactly supported probability measure. This obstruction uses the equal-scale and equal-mass structure of finitely many disjoint affine copies of the measure, together with Parseval's identity and an elementary atom bound for positive measures. We apply it to prove that the golden-mean self-similar measure generated by $x/2$ and $(x+2)/4$ is non-spectral. Together with a weight-rigidity argument, this excludes spectrality for every positive choice of weights in this iterated function system. We also analyze a logarithmically incommensurable example generated by $x/2$ and $(x+2)/3$, proving non-spectrality for all first-branch weights $p\in[1/3,5/6]$, including the natural weights. The latter proof reduces to two finite, exactly checkable integer difference-set conditions; an independent verification program is included in the paper.

papers.title: An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model
papers.abstract: TRIBE v2 (d'Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE's video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2's predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.

papers.title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
papers.abstract: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.

papers.title: Reproduction of Simulated Acoustics Scenes Using Acoustics Room Transformer for speech intelligibility tests in Clinics
papers.abstract: An Acoustic Room Transformation (ART) method is proposed for clinical applications to render simulated acoustic environments using six loudspeakers in a reverberant room. In typical clinical settings, testing rooms are not acoustically treated and only a limited number of loudspeakers are available. The ART approach enables control of the playback-room reverberation, allowing speech intelligibility tests to be performed under realistic and perceptually compensated conditions. The method focuses on the two most common Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) configurations: S0N90 and S0N90. One front and one side loudspeaker reproduce the direct sound components, while the remaining four loudspeakers (two in front and two behind the listener) generate the reverberant sound field. The direct sound is optimized in terms of energy, and the reverberant field is adjusted based on both energy and interaural coherence. An additional direct-sound gain is applied to match the clarity index (C50) of the reproduced signals to that of the reference target. Results from speech intelligibility tests demonstrate that, with ART processing, the reproduced scenarios achieve SRT values very close to those of the reference signal in both S0N0 and S0N90 conditions and therefore allow for comparable speech test results independent of the particular test room acoustics.

papers.title: Singularly embedded solitons and Stokes phenomenon in the fifth order KdV equation
papers.abstract: We study embedded solitons (ES) in a fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation near a reversible Hamiltonian saddle-centre bifurcation. The solitons correspond to homoclinic orbits to an equilibrium whose linearisation has a pair of real and a pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues. Existence of symmetric homoclinic near the bifurcation is a codimension-one phenomenon governed by a parameter-dependent Stokes constant associated with an inner equation. Using complex matching, we derive an oscillatory large-parameter asymptotic formula for the Stokes constant. This formula implies the existence of a countable sequence of zeros and gives their asymptotic distribution in parameter space. We also develop two complementary high-precision numerical procedures for evaluating the Stokes constant: one based on the late terms of the formal inner expansion and another on direct computation of the stable and unstable manifolds. The numerical results agree with each other and with the asymptotic prediction, confirming both the existence and the predicted locations of the embedded-soliton branches.

papers.title: KnowVis: Dual-View Evaluation and Diagnosis of World-Knowledge Grounding in Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.

papers.title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
papers.abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

papers.title: EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $π^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($π^3$) matches the success rate of $π^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($π^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

papers.title: Do Machines Learn Deviance From Their Peers? A Randomized Test of Differential Association With AI Agents
papers.abstract: Differential association theory and its extension, social learning theory, hold that rule-breaking, and the definitions that make it acceptable, are learned through interaction with others. Because people choose their friends, this claim has been hard to test. We addressed this selection problem with AI agents, which learn only through communication and can be assigned to peers at random. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three agents (1,260 agents; seven AI models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly. A scripted teammate said that it had cheated (deviant peer), that it had reported the problem honestly (honest peer), or said nothing (silent peer). Half of the teams were told that an auditor read their chat. Compared with a silent peer, a deviant peer increased cheating (66.2% vs. 62.9%; OR = 1.96) and an honest peer reduced it (55.7%; OR = 0.35). Among agents that cheated, a deviant peer increased claims that cheating was normal (13.7% vs. 3.4%), often as the team's norm. Monitoring did not suppress prohibited discussion; it doubled it. Peers mattered only for models that had not yet decided. AI agents offer a new way to test criminological learning theories without selection effects.

papers.title: AG-JEPA: Anatomically Guided Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Neurodegenerative Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Brain MRI can reveal early signs of Alzheimers disease (AD) before measurable cognitive decline becomes apparent. However, during the transition from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), the disease-related signals are often subtle and confined to only a few brain regions. Existing Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models learn general structural representations but do not explicitly capture the anatomical regions affected in AD. We propose Anatomically Guided JEPA (AG-JEPA), which introduces anatomical tokens that interact with patch tokens during pretraining to learn region-specific representations from brain regions relevant to neurodegeneration. Building on this representation space, we further propose Prog-AG-JEPA, which models disease progression trajectory as a conditioned latent displacement within this space. We evaluate AG-JEPA across five downstream tasks spanning Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and progression prediction. AG-JEPA improves diagnosis and MCI prognosis, achieving an 8.4 percentage point AUROC gain over the strongest baseline on CN/MCI classification and a 7.1 percentage point gain on out-of-distribution CN/AD classification on the MR-RATE dataset, highlighting its effectiveness across both early-stage detection and cross-cohort generalization. For disease progression modeling, Prog-AG-JEPA consistently outperforms all baselines on future diagnosis and brain volume change prediction, demonstrating the value of anatomically grounded neurodegeneration representations for diagnosis and prognosis.

papers.title: VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via mid-layer cross-modal attention, then constructs preference pairs that share the same correct answer but differ in evidence sufficiency (full image vs.\ key-region masked image). Direct preference optimization on these pairs encourages low-resource inputs to prefer answers supported by complete visual evidence. Experiments on multilingual POPE and MME with Chinese, French, and Hindi show consistent hallucination reduction and perception gains, with the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language. Analyses further confirm that VEPO sharpens question-relevant attention and that evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.

papers.title: Training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression with varying correlation scales
papers.abstract: The scale parameter in kernel ridge regression plays a pivotal role in modeling the correlation structure of data. In modern applications, sampling density and the underlying correlation range often change simultaneously, making a fixed-scale assumption highly restrictive. However, establishing asymptotic theories under varying scale parameters is fundamentally challenging. To address this gap, this paper develops a unified theoretical framework for kernel ridge regression under varying scale parameters. We establish that, on uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the consistency of the training-point risk holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity. This sharp criterion universally covers all regimes along arbitrary deterministic scale sequences, seamlessly unifying the long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range. Furthermore, we provide an explicit, signal-independent construction of a deterministic regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency. Numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and the corresponding penalty across all the three regimes.

papers.title: Controllability-Informed Distributed Electric Propulsion Aircraft Design Using Probabilistic Attainable Moment Sets
papers.abstract: Integrated aircraft design combines models of aerodynamics, propulsion, mass, and mission performance in one design loop, so that the disciplines can be traded against each other from the earliest stage. For configurations with distributed electric propulsion (DEP), part of the control authority comes from the propulsion system itself, which directly affects the required size of the tail and should therefore be known while the aircraft is being sized. This paper presents a controllability measure that is evaluated for every design in the loop and returned to it as a design signal. The attainable moment set of each candidate design is computed from the surrugate models of the loop and it is compared with a required moment set. Since the low-fidelity surrugate models are uncertain, the comparison is formulated with probabilistic attainable moment sets: the uncertainty is propagated to the boundary of the set, which yields a margin for every direction in the moment space and the probability of violating the requirement. The design loop thereby informed whether a configuration provides sufficient control authority, on which axes it falls short, and how this changes with the design variables. The approach is demonstrated on a DEP regional aircraft, where the signal is used to assess the size of the vertical tail.

papers.title: Finite-Larmor-radius vortex interaction from δf to full-f gyrofluid dynamics
papers.abstract: We study finite-size electrostatic gyrofluid vortex pairs in a two-dimensional isothermal model, focusing on finite-Larmor-radius effects and the transition from local perturbative to finite-amplitude full-distribution dynamics. An effective response kernel based on Padé ion gyroaveraging regularizes the short-range Euler interaction on the Larmor-radius scale while preserving its logarithmic far field, yielding a finite- core prediction for the orbital frequency. Local-model scans show that increasing the ion temperature relative to the electron temperature enhances gyrospinning and filamentation and drives a separation-dependent transition from merger to long-lived co-rotation. Long-wavelength simulations reproduce the predicted finite-Larmor- radius-induced dip in orbital angular frequency, corresponding to a pronounced slowdown of the vortex-pair rotation. For the full-distribution regime, we introduce a quasi-neutrality-consistent initialization that reconstructs the ion gyrocenter density from prescribed electron density and electrostatic potential. It recovers the local limit at small amplitude, whereas finite-amplitude simulations reveal additional mean-density polarization vorticity, delayed or arrested merger, and a loss of density- vorticity sign symmetry already in the cold-ion full-f system. An independent sign scan of density and vorticity then shows how this nonlinear NOB asymmetry combines with the local warm-ion FLR symmetry breaking identified in earlier δf vortex studies; for warm ions, Padé-based arbitrary-wavelength NOB and NOB+LWL polarization additionally produce distinct morphologies and trajectories. These results demonstrate that nonlinear density-dependent polarization and FLR physics form separate but coupled mechanisms that can qualitatively alter elementary vortex interactions in two-dimensional gyrofluid dynamics.

papers.title: Beyond Scalar Inertia: Frequency-Response-Based Assessment of Finite-Duration Inertial Support in Grid-Forming Converters
papers.abstract: Conventional scalar inertia characterizes only the low-frequency terminal behavior of grid-forming converters (GFMs) and cannot fully predict inertial energy delivery during short-duration frequency disturbances. This letter proposes a frequency-response-based method to assess finite-duration inertial support using complex terminal power--frequency responses, such as those provided by Network Frequency Perturbation (NFP) plots. For GFMs with nonzero steady-state droop, a duration-dependent energy-equivalent inertia is defined after subtracting the ideal static-droop contribution. An exact spectral relationship is established, expressing this metric as a duration-weighted integral of frequency-dependent inertia, without requiring knowledge of the internal controller structure and parameters. The duration dependence of the metric is further shown to encode observable oscillation frequencies and damping ratios. A coefficient-decoupling GFM control with identical scalar inertia and droop across different settings is used for verification.

papers.title: Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications
papers.abstract: Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones. Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of $(j-1)$ quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of $j$ registers (of $n_{qb}$ qubits each) using a mere $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ $\mathtt{CNOT}$ and single-qubit gates, and $3j+\lceil\log_2j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''. The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of \cite{Galvez-Viruet:2024hry} by almost two powers of $j$ and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.

papers.title: Bound-preserving finite volume scheme for a coupled parabolic system with nonlinear and nonlocal drift
papers.abstract: We propose a bound preserving finite-volume scheme for a coupled system of partial differential equations with nonlinear, nonlocal drift. The main contribution of this work is twofold: $(1)$ we show that the proposed scheme preserves physically motivated bounds; $(2)$ we prove that the scheme is well-posed and leads to a sequence of approximate solutions converging to the weak solution of the original problem. This setting is motivated by questions related to morphology formation in organic solar cells.

papers.title: Deep Latents, Long Memory: Latent persistence explains temporal correlations in transformer activations
papers.abstract: The hidden layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) are believed to encode representations of the data whose abstraction increases with depth. However, in the absence of an operational notion of abstraction, this statement is hard to test quantitatively. Here, we propose an alternative view, building on the principle that the correlations of a sequence reflect the structure of the process that generated it. We define the autocorrelation function of a layer as the average dot product between its activations at two context positions separated by a lag. Latent variables encoded persistently along the context create slowly decaying tails in the autocorrelation, and we find these tails to grow across layers in both synthetic and natural data. In synthetic data with controlled hierarchical latent structure, this growth stems from the encoding of abstract latent variables, which govern long stretches of the input. Indeed, the persistence of latent codes predicts the qualitative structure of autocorrelations and accounts for most of the empirical measures. In real text, we take sparse-autoencoder features as proxies for latent variables, and find that their persistence correlates strongly with the magnitude of autocorrelations across datasets and LLMs. In particular, the persistence time increases with depth, as do autocorrelations, implying that deeper latent features persist for longer context spans. We complement this analysis by explicitly ablating the persistent sparse-autoencoder features and observing a consequent decrease in the autocorrelations.

papers.title: Two-Clustering Regime of Token Dynamics in Causal Attention
papers.abstract: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $λ_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $λ_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $λ_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Our theoretical findings are illustrated through simulations and experimental studies using Group Query Attention (GQA) layers.

papers.title: On the convergence of the False Nearest Neighbours algorithm
papers.abstract: The False Nearest Neighbours (FNN) algorithm is one of the most widely used methods for choosing the embedding dimension, i.e. the number $k$ of delay coordinates, in the time-delay reconstruction of a dynamical system from an observed scalar time series. We prove rigorous results on the behaviour of this algorithm for long time series. We consider a smooth dynamical system on a compact manifold $M$ and an invariant probability measure $μ$. For a typical measurement function and $μ$-almost every trajectory, we show that the proportion of false nearest neighbours tends to zero (provided that the tolerance threshold is large enough) once $k >\dim M$. On the other hand, for systems with super-polynomial decay of correlations, we prove that this proportion tends to one whenever $k$ is smaller than the Hausdorff dimension of $μ$. Consequently, in this case, the FNN algorithm (run for long enough time series) returns an embedding dimension $k$ satisfying $\dim_H μ\leq k \leq \dim M + 1$. This is below the threshold $2\dim M + 1$ required by the Takens embedding theorem, so the classical Takens embedding theory does not explain why reconstructions and predictions with $k$ chosen by the FNN algorithm work in practice. The explanation for this case is provided by a recent probabilistic theory of time-delay embeddings. We apply our results to the Hénon and Lorenz attractors, showing that the FNN algorithm typically returns $k=2$ for the Hénon map (in the chaotic case) and $k \leq 3$ for the Lorenz system.

papers.title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
papers.abstract: When a government increases public spending on tertiary (university) education, does it provide a positive fiscal return on investment once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests that model four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up economic growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student university spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (93% probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (96% probability). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond as cohorts graduate: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (89% probability) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (90% probability) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (100% probability) after five-year within-country funding increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (95% probability) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (98% probability) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one entering cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career tax payments shows a typical three- to five-fold total tax return in high-income economies (EUR 2.37 billion in Ireland returning EUR 9.66 billion in total tax with a 77% probability of net profit and EUR 2.87 billion in direct income tax, or EUR 11.55 billion in the UK returning EUR 58.33 billion), whereas expanding the university budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.

papers.title: Distributed Output-Feedback Control for Linear Multichannel Systems
papers.abstract: This paper investigates distributed output-feedback stabilization of linear multichannel systems in which agents exchange state estimates without disclosing local control inputs or feedback gains. Remote control actions are treated as unknown inputs and geometrically decoupled from stable quotient-error dynamics.
