Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.

papers.title: Invariance Preserving Conjugation and Linear Operators on the Hardy Space
papers.abstract: We study linear and anti-linear operators on the Hardy space $H^2$ in connection with the Beurling lattice. First, in contrast to Sarason's result \cite{S1}, we show that no non-zero anti-linear operator leaves every shift-invariant subspace invariant. Then we completely characterize the class of conjugations, isometries, and invertible linear operators preserving the shift-invariant subspace structure in terms of weighted composition operators induced by disk automorphisms--combined with the canonical conjugation, isometric multiplication, and invertible Toeplitz operators, respectively. We also establish the existence and non-existence of conjugations that map shift-invariant subspaces to coinvariant subspaces. Finally, we construct a counterexample that rules out an analogous factorization for bounded linear operators preserving shift-invariance of closed images.

papers.title: Medical Image Segmentation based on Deep Active Contour and Mean Curvature Loss Function
papers.abstract: Pixel-level supervision in medical image segmentation ignores the geometric priors of the target region. Chan-Vese losses restore region-level priors and boundary regularity but do not characterise local boundary geometry. We propose the Deep Active Contour and Mean Curvature (DACMC) loss, which embeds the mean curvature of the predicted boundary in the Chan-Vese region functional; a fixed fourth-order-accurate convolution kernel evaluates curvature without explicit differentiation. The loss adds no trainable parameters and no inference cost, increases training time by 4.8%, and uses one hyper-parameter lambda = 10^-3 shared by all settings. We evaluate DACMC on liver CT, spleen MRI and ISIC dermoscopy images with U-Net and CE-Net backbones, four metrics (DSC, HD95, JS, ASD) and four competing losses under an identical protocol, together with a five-point lambda sweep, a wall-clock cost measurement and a five-seed replication with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. DACMC ranks first or second in Dice in five of the six dataset-backbone settings, most consistently in distance metrics. On spleen MRI it reduces HD95 and ASD to 16.28 and 1.90 mm, and on ISIC dermoscopy it reduces HD95 to 7.08 mm. Dice varies by 0.0023 across five lambda values spanning three orders of magnitude; degradation appears only when curvature dominates. Five-seed replication shows that curvature stabilises training and removes occasional severe failures, although mean differences from the closest competing loss do not reach statistical significance at five seeds. DACMC imposes second-order geometric regularity on segmentation boundaries at low overhead, with the clearest benefit for small or scale-varying targets. Limitations include dataset size and partitioning, classical backbones and losses, and restriction to 2-D single-organ images.

papers.title: When Can Learned Uncertainty Be Trusted? An Audit of Distributional Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Many learned predictive models represent their uncertainty as a probability distribution, and planners and policies use this distribution to judge risk. However, the fact that a model outputs a distribution does not tell us whether that distribution captures the uncertainty in the environment which is relevant for a decision. In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_θ(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. Based on these results, we suggest that uncertainty estimates, including those of learned world models, should be checked against realized outcomes at the decisions where they are used..

papers.title: Reformation of Supercritical Perpendicular Shock
papers.abstract: Super-critical collisionless shocks are not static but evolve continuously as they reflect incoming ions upstream. The process responsible for this non-stationarity -- whether wave-like corrugation of the shock surface (rippling) or cyclic rebuilding of the shock transition (reformation) -- remains debated. We combine Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) observations of a nearly perpendicular ($θ_{Bn}\approx89^\circ$), supercritical ($M_A\approx6$) bow shock with a high-resolution two-dimensional hybrid simulation. MMS reveals repeated ion phase-space holes and intense, localized Hall electric fields. A virtual-spacecraft analysis of the simulation reproduces these signatures and shows that they arise from a self-regulating feedback cycle: strong Hall-field ion reflection builds a reflected-ion foot, which weakens the Hall field and suppresses further reflection until the foot decays and the cycle restarts. This reformation cycle, spatially organized by the two-dimensional shock structure, can account for several principal signatures of the observed non-stationarity.

papers.title: The fixed boundary plasma equilibrium basis for a one Gigawatt electric stellarator power plant
papers.abstract: A fixed boundary stellarator equilibrium capable of producing 3 GW of fusion power (1 GW-electric) is presented as the design basis for the GIGA fusion power plant being developed by Gauss Fusion GmbH. The stellarator concept provides a steady-state, transient free, low recirculating power approach to a fusion power plant, which builds on 50 years of progress in plasma physics. A set of requirements for a fixed boundary equilibrium were determined through application of 0.5 D modeling. Optimization of a modified Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) equilibrium was performed to achieve these requirements including alpha power confinement greater than $85\%$, neoclassical effective ripple below 0.01, bootstrap current below 50 kA, and reduced turbulent heat fluxes. In order to fix the plasma volume of $1500~m^3$ during optimization, the VMEC code was modified to renormalize the boundary coefficient to the desired plasma volume. The STELLOPT stellarator optimization code was modified as well to include new bootstrap current targets, a new target for the radial electric field, and the capability to hold the magnetic field on axis at a fixed value. An intermediary conceptual design plasma and final evolved fixed boundary equilibria are compared to the original modified W7-X equilibrium. The final evolved equilibrium is shown to achieve all the necessary requirements for the GIGA fusion power plant through more detailed modeling of stability, fast ion confinement, and transport.

papers.title: AI Search as an Information Intermediary: Clickstream Evidence on Web Traffic
papers.abstract: AI search retrieves web information to ground generated answers. We study this new information intermediary using U.S. desktop clickstream data observing use alongside referrals during ChatGPT Search's rollout. Referrals accompany 5.4% of ChatGPT sessions versus 31.1% of Google queries. Ad-supported sites receive a smaller share of ChatGPT than Google referrals, while reference and technical sites receive larger shares. Conventional searches (Google, Bing, Yahoo) decline after ChatGPT adoption, sooner when adoption follows ChatGPT Search's expansion to users without accounts. Among existing users, that expansion raises ChatGPT use; conventional searches show no detectable overall change but fall among households with lower prior search activity. These findings suggest AI search can reshape open-web traffic through its own referrals and changes in conventional search.

papers.title: Reduction Types of Genus 2 Curves
papers.abstract: Tate produced a table for elliptic curves over local fields that beautifully summarises their arithmetic invariants in terms of the Kodaira type. We present an analogous set of tables for curves of genus 2. The invariants addressed include: reduction type of the minimal regular model, reduction type of the minimal regular model with normal crossings, Néron component group of the Jacobian, conductor exponent, valuation of the discriminant of a minimal Weierstrass model, and cluster pictures.

papers.title: DiffCVE: Diffusion-based Compressed Video Enhancement
papers.abstract: Perceptual quality enhancement of severely compressed videos remains challenging due to complex artifact patterns and substantial information loss. Recent diffusion models have demonstrated strong generative capability for visual restoration, but directly applying them to compressed video often ignores compression degradation characteristics and may introduce structure-inconsistent hallucinations. To address this issue, this paper presents a diffusion-based compressed video enhancement method, named DiffCVE. Coding Prior-enhanced Dual Conditioning (CPDC) branches are designed to jointly model compressed video and coding prior conditions, where coding priors including residuals and motion vectors provide complementary structural and motion guidance during the diffusion denoising process. To make the diffusion process aware of compression severity, a Compression Degradation Semantic Prompting (CDSP) mechanism is introduced to leverage QP-conditioned textual prompts together with LoRA fine-tuning. In addition, a Coding Prior-guided Weighted Fusion (CPWF) module is incorporated into the VAE decoder to fuse VAE encoder and coding prior encoder features with QP-predicted weights. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving perceptual quality, especially under severe compression settings. The project page and code are available at https://wqmaker.github.io/projects/DiffCVE/.

papers.title: Is the Geometry Doing the Work? An Operating-Point Audit of Hierarchy in Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are designed to encode abstraction geometrically: general concepts near the origin, specific ones farther out, and entailment cones representing directed order. We ask whether trained MERU, HyCoCLIP, and PHyCLIP models actually use these mechanisms. We audit seven released checkpoints and matched from-scratch interventions. All audited converged checkpoints remain near-Euclidean in the dimensionless radius $u=\sqrt{c}ρ$: the largest observed image-side value is $0.37$ -- well below $u\approx0.84$, where local metric distortion reaches $10\%$. Releasing the curvature floor changes curvature and norms but not this regime, with mixed, generally modest downstream shifts. Trained entailment cones are saturated or nearly saturated, so low violation rates can arise from trivially wide cones rather than learned order. Preregistered semantic traversal detects weak within-branch order but no operative full-hierarchy readout. Shuffle-controlled tests detect no pair-specific radial ordering in released checkpoints, and no positive result is consistent across all three matched ViT-B seeds. This non-detection is sensitivity-bounded: the diagnostic reaches $80\%$ power only at $\approx13.5$ pp of shuffle-controlled excess, while the largest released gap is $\approx5$ pp. We trace this to a low-curvature shortcut: lowering curvature widens entailment cones and suppresses violations without learning order. In the probed trajectories, gradient decomposition identifies entailment as the dominant curvature-lowering pressure during collapse. Yet curvature contracts even when entailment is removed, so the shortcut is not the sole cause. Under our diagnostics, the audited formulations do not demonstrate an operative radial or cone-based hierarchy. We distill the audit into a five-number geometry report for evaluating future hierarchy claims.

papers.title: Physically-Relevant Information Learning in High-Dimensional Time-Derivatives Spaces
papers.abstract: Understanding the physics of many-body complex dynamical systems may be a non-trivial task. High-dimensional analysis approaches are often deemed necessary to prevent losing important information. Typically, these use order parameters or descriptors capturing information related to, e.g., relative positions, symmetries, etc., of the units in the studied system. However, in many cases, gaining information related to the relative positions of the constitutive units (or their velocities) alone may be insufficient, and to reach a more complete physical knowledge, one should ideally learn and correlate with each other both structure and dynamics. Here we demonstrate how to achieve such a goal efficiently by building and navigating high-dimensional Time-Derivatives (TiDe) spaces. A TiDe space can be generated for virtually any type of system/phenomenon from the time-series data collected along its observation over time. Each TiDe's dimension corresponds to a growing-order time-derivative of the extracted data, thus containing information related to different physical phenomena/events, which can be easily extracted via unsupervised approaches. We demonstrate how, by definition, TiDes can be directly analyzed without a need for prior dimensionality reduction, providing results that are intrinsically intuitive to interpret. We show the potential of the method by analyzing two prototypical example datasets extracted from molecular dynamics simulations or experimental tracking of different types of complex dynamical systems. Our results demonstrate how efficiently one can navigate and learn in information-rich TiDe spaces, which provide a robust general framework for data analysis and for studying complex dynamical systems from the data collected along their observation over time.

papers.title: A unified approach to cross-intersection problems with applications to Hilton--Milner type theorems and stability
papers.abstract: We develop a new approach to cross-intersection problems in extremal set theory. The method builds on the iterative procedure introduced by Kupavskii and Zakharov (2024) and the $t$-cover method. It provides a flexible framework for deriving extremal and stability results for cross $t$-intersecting families. Our approach applies to a variety of combinatorial objects. As an application, we prove a product version of the seminal Erdős--Ko--Rado theorem for sufficiently spread set systems. Two families $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ of $k$-subsets of $[n]$ are called cross $t$-intersecting if $|F\cap G|\geq t$ for all $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and $G\in\mathcal{G}$. We determine the families maximizing $\min\{|\mathcal{F}|, |\mathcal{G}|\}$ for large $n$ and all $t\ge2$, generalizing results of Mörs (1985) and Füredi (1995) for cross $1$-intersecting families. We then determine the families maximizing $|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{G}|$ under the condition $\max\{|\cap_{F\in\mathcal{F}}F|,|\cap_{G\in\mathcal{G}}G|\}<t$ for large $n$. This improves the bound obtained by Frankl and Wang (2024), and provides a characterization of extremal configurations. For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$, we introduce its $t$-diversity $γ_t(\mathcal{F})$, defined as the minimum number of sets from $\mathcal{F}$ not containing a fixed $t$-subset. This serves as a natural generalization of the important notion of diversity for $t=1$. We obtain a stability result via $γ_t$, and determine the maximum of $\min\{γ_t(\mathcal{F}),γ_t(\mathcal{G})\}$ for cross $t$-intersecting families $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$. These yield new results for $t$-intersecting families, including a stability theorem towards a conjecture of Ellis, Keller and Lifshitz (2019), which may also be regarded as a $t$-intersection version, for large $n$, of an influential theorem of Frankl (1987).

papers.title: Numerical analysis of the Biot equations coupled to frictional contact mechanics
papers.abstract: We consider a mathematical model of a poroviscoelastic medium subject to frictional contact with a rigid obstacle, and study its numerical approximation. This model couples the Biot equations and contact conditions in the form of normal compliance and Coulomb friction. The resulting variational problem consists of a linear partial differential equation coupled to a nonlinear variational inequality. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution is established, and stability and a priori error estimates are derived. A numerical experiment is performed in which numerical error estimates are computed and compared to the theoretical results.

papers.title: Fast approximation and learning of binary classification tasks in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks
papers.abstract: We study binary classification tasks whose decision sets are given by definable sets in o-minimal expansions of the real field. Motivated by the cell decomposition theory of definable sets, we introduce traceable sets that isolate the analytical properties of definable sets used for fast approximation by ReLU neural networks. Under uniform bounds on the number of cells and a suitable extension assumption for the boundary functions, we prove that classifiers can be approximated in $L^p$ up to accuracy $\varepsilon>0$ by ReLU neural networks of size $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-p(n-1)/m})$, with depth independent of $\varepsilon$ and polynomially bounded weights. This establishes quantitative approximation rates for suitable definable collections in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks. Furthermore, the stated approximation rates are also derived for definable maps under similar geometric assumptions on their smoothness domains. We then obtain statistical learning rates for empirical risk minimization with hinge loss over the approximating ReLU neural network classes. For $N$ uniformly distributed samples, the predicted classifiers achieve expected misclassification error of order $N^{-m/(m+n-1)}$ up to an arbitrarily small polynomial loss.

papers.title: Horizon-scale intensity and polarization images of rotating Konoplya-Zhidenko black holes with thick accretion flows
papers.abstract: We investigate the shadow and polarization images of a Konoplya--Zhidenko rotating non-Kerr black hole surrounded by a geometrically thick and optically thin accretion flow. The accretion flow is described by an analytical ballistic approximation accretion flow model. The numerical results show that the shadow image exhibits two main features, an outer bright ring and an inner dark region. The former corresponds to higher-order images, while the latter is associated with photon capture by the black hole. Increasing the deformation parameter $η$ does not significantly change the overall shape of the higher-order images, but it enlarges their size. Increasing either the spin parameter $a$ or the observer inclination angle $θ_o$ enhances the asymmetry of the higher-order images and makes the intensity on the left side much larger than that on the right side. This behavior is associated with frame dragging and the relativistic Doppler effect. In the polarization images, the degree of linear polarization is much smaller in the higher-order image region than in other regions, and the polarization vectors extend over the whole image plane. Within the framework used in this work, these results illustrate how the spacetime geometry and near-horizon accretion dynamics jointly influence the intensity and polarization images.

papers.title: SimpleSearch-VL: A Simple Recipe for Multimodal Agentic Deep Search
papers.abstract: We present SimpleSearch-VL, an efficient, reliable, and practical framework for multimodal agentic search. Its core idea is to improve the agent's own search-and-verification process rather than scaling data, tools, or auxiliary model components. For efficiency, Factorized Adaptive Rollout (FAR) improves sampling efficiency by forming more informative training groups while using redundant samples to mitigate long-tail latency and expose hard samples. For reliability, SimpleSearch-VL performs evidence-verified reasoning, explicitly using chain-of-thought verification to assess the relevance of retrieved visual and textual cues to the original context. For practicality, SimpleSearch-VL keeps a lightweight tool interface and performs webpage self-summary within the agent, requiring no additional external dependencies. With only 5K supervised tool-interleaved trajectories and 2K RL data, SimpleSearch-VL improves Qwen3-VL agentic baselines by 15.8 and 16.0 average points for the 8B and 30B-A3B variants, respectively. The SimpleSearch-VL-30B-A3B model further achieves performance competitive with agentic Gemini-3-Pro.

papers.title: Graph-Spectral Entanglement
papers.abstract: We introduce a unified graph-spectral framework for quantifying multipartite entanglement, built upon an entanglement graph and its associated entanglement matrix. The framework accommodates general subsystem and partition structures of composite quantum systems, while offering a complementary geometric and network perspective on characterizing multipartite quantum correlations. We prove that the resulting graph-spectral entanglement satisfies the requirements of an entanglement measure. Furthermore, we derive a multipartite monogamy relation and, based on the resulting spectral hierarchy, introduce residual graph-spectral entanglement for arbitrary multipartite states. This establishes a general construction of residual entanglement beyond conventional qubit-based formulations and provides a new approach to investigating, quantifying, witnessing, and classifying multipartite entanglement in both theoretical and experimental settings.

papers.title: World-Model Collapse as a Phase Transition
papers.abstract: Water looks unchanged as it warms, then at a critical point it boils. We ask whether long-horizon language agents show an analogous transition in their ability to maintain an accurate representation of the evolving world state. In some parameter settings, a small change in a task parameter, or adding a single step to the task, leaves behavior nearly unchanged; near a critical boundary, the same small change causes a sudden collapse. We study this effect in a deterministic task family where the true world state is known at every step. A large grid search over state size, state dependency, horizon, number of available actions, observation mode, and frequency of state changes reveals a phase diagram: a low-stress region where the agent consistently succeeds, a narrow region where success drops sharply, and a high-stress region where the agent consistently fails. Step-by-step traces show the mechanism: the agent loses track of the true world before its actions become invalid, so the agent is not merely choosing a bad action; it is acting from a corrupted world. Stronger models reach the critical boundary later but do not eliminate the sharp transition. These results make world-model collapse a measurable bottleneck for long-horizon agents. Code will be made publicly available soon.

papers.title: The Decomposition Is the Fingerprint: Per-Component Identity for Agent Skills
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly acquire and execute skills at runtime: bundles of prompt instructions, executable code, and tool declarations fetched from marketplaces and other agents. Governing them needs a stable notion of skill identity, yet cryptographic hashing is engineered to destroy the very similarity we need, as a one-character edit scrambles the digest. We present a compact, locality-sensitive fingerprint that embeds each component of a skill and projects it to bits with a multi-bank SimHash, giving a fixed 120-byte signature compared in constant time by Hamming distance. Our central claim is that keeping the fingerprint as a per-component triple (prompt, code, tools), rather than a single score, is what makes it useful: the triple recovers skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component remains shared, while independent multilingual reimplementation is not recovered; it also localizes which component carries the reuse. We claim lineage, not behavioral equivalence: identity supplies the structural axis of a registry and leaves safety to behavioral verification. The fingerprint reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons while using 77x fewer bits than the embedding it approximates, with ranking preserved in expectation and finite-bit concentration; the per-component split turns one number into relationship classification, families, novelty, and a portable "SkillBOM" for a skill registry. On a 906-skill injection benchmark the fingerprint recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the change, but recognition is not trust: it remains, by design, an identity signal complementary to behavioral verification rather than a safety verdict.

papers.title: Power-integral matrices over number fields: the Drazin inverse, pseudo-determinant, and numerical semigroups
papers.abstract: We investigate matrices with entries in a number field such that some positive power has all its entries in the corresponding ring of integers. Our work generalizes previous results in several directions and we find applications to numerical semigroups.

papers.title: Thermal Double-Twist Data in Holography
papers.abstract: We explain how to extract thermal OPE coefficients of double-twist operators in scalar two-point functions at infinite spatial volume from suitably regularized integrals of thermal response functions in momentum space. As a specific application, we implement the proposed approach to four-dimensional holographic CFTs with an Einstein bulk action, where the finite-temperature state is captured by an AdS$_5$ black-brane geometry. In that case, the thermal response function can be computed on the gravitational side by solving numerically a radial ODE reduction of the Klein-Gordon equation. We obtain accurate values of double-twist data from this solution, completing previous holographic and bootstrap studies of thermal two-point functions. Some of the reported spin-resolved data that we compute are new.

papers.title: Hankel and Multiplication Tensor Completions for Cactus Rank
papers.abstract: We show that the Hankel flat extension formulation of the cactus algorithm is equivalent to a completion problem for multiplication tensors of Artinian Gorenstein algebras. The unknown Hankel moments are canonically identified with the undetermined tensor coefficients, and under this identification the symbolic multiplication matrices and their commutation equations coincide. This shows that the usual degree extension formulation is a coordinate realization of a variable extension problem with marked generators. We further use Borel-fixed and squat staircases to reduce the family of candidate basis shapes in the resulting algorithm.

papers.title: GigaSpeechBench: A Real-World Multilingual Speech-to-Text Benchmark
papers.abstract: While modern ASR systems achieve low error rates on high-resource benchmarks, such performance often overestimates real-world robustness. Existing evaluations address challenges in isolation, lacking a unified benchmark for domain terminology, age variation, dialects, accents, and low-resource languages, particularly across the Middle East and Southeast Asia, representing over one billion under-evaluated speakers. To address this gap, we introduce GigaSpeechBench, a comprehensive multilingual and multidimensional in-the-wild ASR & AST benchmark comprising 690 hours of human-annotated speech. It features five modules: (1) 12 low-resource Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian languages, plus challenging Japanese and Korean; (2) 6 Chinese dialects; (3) 6 English accents; (4) dense terminology across 12 vertical domains for Chinese and English; and (5) older adult and child speech. We further provide human-annotated Chinese and English translations for 11 languages to support AST evaluation. Extensive evaluations of leading foundation models and commercial APIs reveal significant performance degradation in these challenging settings, exposing critical evaluation blind spots.

papers.title: Scaling limit of the Random Language Model
papers.abstract: We develop a quantitative theory of the Random Language Model (RLM), an ensemble of stochastic context-free grammars, in a scaling limit where the number of hidden symbols $N \to \infty$ while the grammar temperature $\tildeε_d \to 0$ at fixed $x = \tildeε_d \log N$. In this limit, the model admits a controlled description based on a large-deviation principle over rule-usage patterns. A semi-annealed approximation maps the problem to a class of Random Energy Models with nontrivial combinatorics. We show that the RLM exhibits a freezing transition at a critical value $x_c=1/8$, below which rule usage condenses on a subset of preferred rules and language statistics acquire a nontrivial dependence on corpus length. A second characteristic scale at $x=1/2$, associated with the breakdown of Gaussian fluctuations, separates transition and babbling regimes. Across regimes, we derive explicit scaling laws for the number of distinct rules, entropy, and energy, identifying distinct frozen and critical regimes controlled by the interplay of grammar size, corpus length, and temperature. The theory resolves previous ambiguities regarding the existence of a thermodynamic transition and explains the slow approach to the large-$N$ limit as a consequence of the dependence on $\log N$. It further provides a unified framework in which universal statistical properties of language emerge from typical realizations of generative grammars, with implications for both natural language statistics and the behavior of large language models. Heaps' law and Zipf's law are both derived, and the dependence of predictive entropy on context length is rationalized. Comparison with empirical measurements of Heaps' and Zipf's laws yields parameter estimates for real languages.

papers.title: Improving General Role-Playing Agents via Psychology-Grounded Reasoning and Role-Aware Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Building general-purpose role-playing agents that faithfully portray any character from a natural-language profile remains challenging. Explicit reasoning can help models deliberate before responding, but generic reasoning does not necessarily preserve character fidelity. We therefore propose Psy-CoT, a psychology-grounded chain-of-thought framework that decomposes pre-response reasoning into three role-specific steps: Interaction Perception, Psychological Empathy, and Logical Construction, so that the model thinks dynamically from the profile rather than merely mimicking surface patterns. While structured reasoning provides a foundation, it alone is insufficient; reinforcement learning is essential to further align the model with character fidelity. However, we observe that under LLM-based reward models, both generic phrases that hack the reward model and genuinely role-specific phrases receive identical gradient signals. This hacking accumulates over training, misleading the model into treating both as equally optimal choices. To address this, we propose Role-Aware Policy Optimization (RAPO), which uses profile-induced entropy differences to weight gradients asymmetrically, amplifying role-specific tokens under positive advantage while attenuating them under negative advantage. Experiments on CoSER, CharacterBench, and CharacterEval demonstrate that Psy-CoT outperforms existing role-playing CoT methods, and RAPO consistently surpasses GRPO across multiple model scales.

papers.title: MiniOpt: Reasoning to Model and Solve General Optimization Problems with Limited Resources
papers.abstract: Achieving strong optimization generalization across diverse optimization problems while requiring limited training resources remains a challenging problem for optimization-oriented large language models (LLMs). Existing learning-based methods, however, typically require large-scale supervised data, expensive intermediate step verification, and extensive computational resources, while exhibiting limited optimization generalization across diverse optimization structures. In this paper, we propose \textsc{MiniOpt}, a lightweight optimization-specialized LLM trained through a reasoning-to-model-and-solve paradigm and a two-stage training framework with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). MiniOpt encourages structure-oriented optimization learning by reinforcing the completeness of optimization formulations and optimization outcomes. Extensive experiments on eight optimization benchmarks demonstrate that MiniOpt consistently outperforms existing learning-based optimization models while requiring substantially fewer parameters and training data. To further understand optimization generalization, we introduce a complementary parameter-decoupled evaluation protocol that disentangles optimization structure understanding from numerical parameter processing. The results reveal that MiniOpt preserves optimization capability under parameter-decoupled settings significantly better than previous optimization-specialized models, suggesting that its performance gains primarily originate from stronger optimization structure understanding. These findings demonstrate an effective pathway toward efficient and generalizable optimization-specialized LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsiang-1/MiniOpt.

papers.title: Translation Continuity and the Structure of Infinite-Dimensional Lebesgue Spaces
papers.abstract: For Baker's Borel-rectangle measure $μ$ and $1\le p<\infty$, we classify the continuous vectors of each one-parameter translation group on $L^p(μ)$. For each $v\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$, the continuous vectors form a projection band, which coincides with the whole space when $v$ has finite support, is trivial when $v\notin\ell^1$, and is nonzero and proper otherwise. We also establish in ZFC the isometric classification considered in [Isometric classification of the $L^{p}$-spaces of infinite dimensional Lebesgue measure, Banach J. Math. Anal. 20 (2026), no. 1, Paper No. 7], showing that both $L^p(μ)$ and the kernel of restriction to integer cubes are lattice isometric to $\ell^p(\mathfrak{c},L^p[0,1])$. When $v\in\ell^1\setminus c_{00}$, the continuous band and its disjoint complement have the same lattice-isometric structure, with the latter contained in the cube-restriction kernel.

papers.title: Hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{H}^2$ with constant sectional curvature
papers.abstract: In this paper, we classify the hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{H}^2$ with constant sectional curvature. In contrast to the case of $\mathbb{S}^2\times\mathbb{S}^2$, the resulting examples for $\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{H}^2$ exhibit greater diversity, and we construct a special example with non-constant product angle function. For $\mathbb{S}^2\times\mathbb{S}^2$, however, the product angle function of any constant sectional curvature hypersurface is identically zero. As a byproduct, we also classify the hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{H}^2$ with constant product angle function and constant mean curvature (or constant scalar curvature).

papers.title: A Universal Telecom-Band Quantum Memory Enabled by Cross-Phase Modulation
papers.abstract: Quantum memories capable of storing and retrieving photonic quantum states on demand are essential for quantum communication, entanglement distribution, and the synchronization of probabilistic quantum processes. All-optical loop-based memories offer broadband operation and compatibility with telecommunication infrastructure, but their performance is often limited by switching losses and the noise introduced by active control mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate a universal all-fiber quantum memory based on two Sagnac interferometers acting as dynamically controlled mirrors through cross-phase modulation. This all-optical switching mechanism enables an input/output transmission as high as 90% (0.46 dB insertion loss), a round-trip transmission of 94.6%, and a characteristic storage lifetime of $18.54 \pm 0.21 μs$. The memory exhibits an operational spectral range exceeding 12.5 THz, while keeping noise to negligible levels across the whole telecom C-band. We experimentally demonstrate the preservation of time-bin-encoded heralded photons and time-bin entanglement, as well as compatibility with polarization- and frequency-bin-encoded optical states. Furthermore, we demonstrate the simultaneous storage of over 200 temporal modes and the selective retrieval of independently addressable modes. Our results establish low-noise switching as a promising approach to broadband quantum memories combining high transmission, encoding versatility, and programmable temporal-mode control.

papers.title: Binary black hole scattering with generic spins
papers.abstract: We study generic-spin black-hole scattering with orbital-plane precession, whose dynamics require more than one scattering angle. From numerical relativity (NR), we extract the polar scattering angle and precession of the orbital plane, the latter characterised by asymptotic Euler angles. A dictionary relating post-Minkowskian (PM) observables to scattering and Euler angles is presented, enabling the first precessing PM-NR comparisons. Our results provide a key benchmark for generic-spin resummations and provide the foundations for exploring boundary-to-bound maps in the generic case.

papers.title: First measurement of narrow-line flux ratios for a lensed quasar with JWST/NIRSpec IFS
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing is a powerful probe of dark matter (DM) structure on subgalactic scales: in particular, statistics of flux-ratio anomalies (discrepancies between mass model predictions and observed flux ratios) in quadruply imaged quasars are sensitive to perturbations by low-mass DM halos down to $\sim 10^6 M_\odot$. Studies leveraging these anomalies require high-quality flux-ratio measurements from an emission region insensitive to stellar microlensing. In this paper, we present the first measurement of narrow-line flux ratios for a gravitationally lensed quasar using JWST/NIRSpec with Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS), targeting the well-studied system RXJ1131$-$1231. Flux ratios are extracted from the [S III] 9071/9533 $Å$ narrow-line doublet - the first use of this doublet for substructure studies - by performing a full lens model reconstruction to isolate the unresolved nuclear emission from extended narrow-line emission. The resulting spectra are jointly modeled using $\texttt{lensqso-specfit}$, a publicly available software package introduced in this work for the simultaneous spectral fitting of multiple lensed quasar images. We achieve $\sim$ 5% uncertainties on the flux ratios, comparable to the precision of JWST/MIRI warm dust measurements, and detect a clear anomaly in the cusp images relative to a standard smooth lens model. Our results are in good agreement with previous narrow-line measurements and broadly consistent with JWST/MIRI warm dust flux ratios, with marginal ($\sim 2-3σ$) deviations. We illustrate how such shifts between differently sized emission regions may be enhanced by small ($\sim 10$ pc) spatial offsets. Our method is generalizable to other systems with existing or future IFS observations, and the combination of narrow-line and warm dust flux ratios offers a new avenue for improving DM constraints with flux-ratio anomaly statistics.

papers.title: On moduli spaces of vector bundles on $K3^{[n]}$-type IHS manifolds
papers.abstract: We study moduli spaces of modular vector bundles on projective irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type. Under suitable numerical assumptions, we exhibit connected components of these moduli spaces which are again irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of $K3^{[n]}$-type. Moreover, the corresponding universal families induce derived equivalences with the original manifolds. This produces smooth components of moduli spaces of modular vector bundles on irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of any even dimension.

papers.title: Scaling of the minimal energy for turbulence transition in pipe flow
papers.abstract: Predicting the transition to turbulence in pipe flow remains a fundamental problem in fluid dynamics. We use a variational approach to compute nonlinear optimal perturbations to the laminar flow. Optimal perturbations are structurally similar for all Reynolds numbers, $1750 \leq Re \leq 10^4$, considered. As $Re$ increases, they increasingly localise in space with thickness scaling as $ Re^{-1/3}$. They grow via the Orr mechanism, followed by a phase of energy transfer across oblique waves of different axial wavenumber, characterised by a rapid delocalisation. The energy gain in the Orr and oblique-wave phases is independent of the initial perturbation energy, $E_0$. Subsequently, rolls grow by nonlinear mechanisms and streaks via the lift-up effect. The energy gain of the (inviscid) Orr phase is independent of the Reynolds number, whereas it increases linearly with $Re$ during the initial oblique-wave phase and quadratically in the roll and lift-up phase. We find that, transition occurs if the energy of the optimal perturbation exceeds a maximum energy threshold during its temporal evolution. This energy is given by the edge state energy and found to be independent of $Re$. As a result, the minimum perturbation energy required to cause transition in pipe flow scales as $E_0^\text{crit}\propto Re^{-3}$, which is consistent with our computation of minimal seeds. We note that insufficiently long pipes lead to an exponent of smaller magnitude and that much larger numerical resolutions are required to accurately compute the energy gain than to compute the critical threshold.

papers.title: Integrating Sensing into Covert Communications: Opportunities and Challenges
papers.abstract: Covert communications aim to hide the existence of wireless transmissions from unauthorized adversaries. However, conventional designs based on blind interference or passive uncertainty can be ineffective in dynamic propagation environments. This article investigates sensing-empowered covert communications, where adversary and environmental information are used to guide transmission and jamming control. We show how sensing changes covert system design from passive concealment to state-aware decision-making, while also introducing new challenges related to exposure and resource consumption. We further discuss several intelligent sensing paradigms that extract task-relevant information with limited active probing. A case study in low-altitude wireless networks illustrates that sensing-assisted beamforming can improve spatial resource utilization and the reliability of covert data delivery in time-varying channels. Finally, several open issues are discussed to support more adaptive covert wireless systems.

papers.title: Nonlinear Static Screening of Positive Charges in an Electron Gas: Contact Hartree Potential
papers.abstract: We investigate nonlinear static screening of a proton in a homogeneous electron gas, focusing on the induced density and contact Hartree potential $V_{\rm H}(0)$, an $r$-weighted moment of the entire screening cloud rather than a strictly local quantity. Thomas--Fermi, RPA, and local-field-corrected linear response are compared with nonlinear DFT-LDA and DFT-PBE calculations. The Estreicher--Meier LDA density fit reproduces the contact Hartree potential closely and resolves its core and Friedel contributions, despite an approximate cusp. Kaplan--Kukkonen and Corradini--Del Sole--Onida--Palummo local-field factors give nearly identical contact predictions for the states examined, without implying general insensitivity to local-field corrections. We extend the variable-phase approach with a companion amplitude equation to reconstruct the quantal induced density from bound and continuum states of constrained screened potentials. Friedel-constrained Yukawa, hydrogenic, and Hulthén potentials satisfy the same total-screening condition but yield different contact densities and Hartree potentials. In the two-parameter Apagyi--Nagy construction, the cusp constrains an auxiliary Poisson density, whereas the reconstructed quantum density obeys the Coulomb cusp automatically; neither the Friedel sum rule nor the cusp uniquely fixes the screening cloud. Model-potential contact results approach nonlinear DFT toward high density but deviate increasingly as $r_s$ grows. By contrast, density-informed Popović--Stott potentials reproduce historical Hartree-only and exchange--correlation-modified contact values within $0.05\%$ without refitting. These findings distinguish global scattering constraints, local cusp behavior, and full-density information, and establish a one-center baseline for future two-center screening calculations.

papers.title: Agent MechSuits: Mechanistic Subspace Safety Steering for Multi-Turn CLI Agents
papers.abstract: Command-Line Interface (CLI) agents based on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable autonomous capabilities, but they also introduce significant safety and misuse risks during multi-turn interactions with external environments. Existing safety mechanisms mainly rely on external guardrails, which have a limited ability to perform fine-grained behavioral control during execution. Meanwhile, recent mechanistic interpretability methods for LLM safety are mostly confined to single-turn or jailbreak-style QA settings, limiting their ability to capture the evolving risk dynamics of multi-turn agent execution. In this paper, we investigate the safety of multi-turn CLI agents from an internal perspective. We propose Agent MechSuits (Mechanistic Subspace Intervention and Steering), a white-box defense framework that performs runtime safety detection and representation-level mitigation for CLI agents. Unlike conventional agent guardrails, Agent MechSuits detects harmful execution states from step-level hidden representations and mitigates unsafe behavior by intervening in a 10-dimensional subspace within a single layer. To support this research, we introduce the Mechanistic Agent Safety (MAS) benchmark, comprising comprehensively annotated multi-turn execution trajectories across 194 tasks using LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Extensive experiments show that Agent MechSuits achieves strong safety detection performance, provides preliminary evidence for lookahead risk anticipation, and substantially reduces harmful actions of the CLI agent, establishing a foundation for applying mechanistic interpretability to dynamic LLM agent safety.

papers.title: A Contradiction Judge Counted Reported Teammate Errors as Hallucinations: An Assertion-Aware Re-Score of One Multi-Agent LLM Harness
papers.abstract: LLM judges that score hallucination flag any statement that contradicts a reference fact. Agents in multi-agent LLM systems quote and dispute each other's claims, so such a judge can count a correct report of a teammate's error as a hallucination. An earlier version of this study, a preprint (arXiv:2606.21666v1), reported that broadcasting raised a hallucination rate from 0.492 to 0.658 (+34%) and called it contamination; this version withdraws that claim, and the preprint's runs cannot be re-scored. An unpublished revision of that harness reported 0.289 to 0.554 (+0.265, 95% CI [0.225, 0.305]), and its saved outputs are re-scored here. Under an analysis plan fixed before any judge call, three judges from three vendors labeled each of six facts in 1,832 outputs as asserted wrong, attributed to another source, asserted correct or absent. On values that outputs assert as their own, the broadcast effect was -0.0208 (95% CI [-0.0458, +0.0041]) on 10 Full-Broadcast trials: not distinguishable from zero, and equivalent to zero only within a post hoc margin of +/-0.0663 and under the plan's prompt. On these LLM-judge labels, reports of a teammate's wrong value accounted for nearly all of the Haiku travel effect. Scored for mentions, the judges reproduced the effect (+0.1996). With Llama agents, 2 of 40 teammate outputs asserted the wrong destination. One of twelve Claude judge-prompt combinations gave an asserted increase (Sonnet 4.6, one paraphrase: +0.0246, 95% CI [+0.0055, +0.0436]). In 40 new trials per arm, judged by Claude models like the agents, the asserted difference was -0.0505 when both judges agreed and +0.0161 (95% CI [+0.0024, +0.0299]) when either did. Main limit: the labels have no human validation; human labels for 120 outputs are pending. The outputs come from one harness and 13 hand-written scenarios, so the shares do not transfer.

papers.title: On the Reachability Problem on Monoid-Labelled Undirected Graphs
papers.abstract: The labelled reachability problem for undirected graphs with edges labelled by elements of a monoid $M$ (more generally, groupoids or magmas) captures the classes $\sf{L}$ and $\sf{NL}$. Given a graph $G(V, E)$ labelled by $ϕ~\colon E \to M$, $s,t \in V$ and an accepting subset $F \subseteq M$, the problem asks to test whether there is a walk $P$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ where $ϕ(P) \in F$. Ramaswamy et al. (2019) studied the variant where the accepting element is part of the input for aperiodic monoids and groups. Motivated by the success in designing space-bounded algorithms for the undirected graph reachability problem, we study the labelled reachability problem when the accepting set is also fixed. This reveals finer complexity bounds and dichotomies for the problem based on the monoid and the accepting set. Previous results imply that the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for any finite accepting subset when $M$ is a group or belongs to $\sf{DA}$. We prove the following (for finite monoids): 1) For any monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ when the accepting element is the identity of $M$. If the accepting element is an idempotent, under suitable constraints, the problem is $\sf{NL}$-hard. 2) For any commutative monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for all $F \subseteq M$. 3) For any $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{R})$-commutative union-of-groups (UoG) monoid $M$, the problem is in $\sf{L}$ for all $F\subseteq M$. We show deterministic logspace algorithms for UoG monoids that are neither $\mathcal{L}$-commutative nor $\mathcal{R}$-commutative, under certain constraints. 4) For the monoids $\sf{BA_2}$ and $\sf{U}$, we show a dichotomy: for all $F \subseteq M$, the problem is either $\sf{NL}$-complete or in $\sf{L}$. Our results exploit the connection between Green's relations in the UoG monoids and the properties of the product graph (a graph introduced by Ramaswamy et al. (2019)).

papers.title: BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems
papers.abstract: LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicated detectors lead. We release the framework, an interactive leaderboard, and four datasets as a vendor-neutral basis for selecting safeguards under deployment constraints.

papers.title: Lagrangian capacity and chain level string topology
papers.abstract: We derive upper bounds for the Lagrangian capacities of Liouville domains with finite Gutt--Hutchings capacities and show that the Lagrangian capacity of a convex or concave toric domain of arbitrary dimension equals its diagonal. In particular, this completely settles the conjecture of Cieliebak-Mohnke on the Lagrangian capacity of ellipsoids. Our proof is based on an $S^1$-equivariant variant of the techniques of Fukaya and Irie, and does not use holomorphic curves with local tangency constraints, which would inevitably cause transversality issues. Moreover, we show that any extremal Lagrangian torus in an $2n$-dimensional ellipsoid must lie on the boundary. Applications of our results and techniques include include a proof of the fact that every monotone Lagrangian torus in the complex projective space has non-trivial intersections with the Clifford torus and the first computations of the Lagrangian capacities for many non-subcritical Weinstein domains in dimensions 4 and 6.

papers.title: Ramping Procurement and Bid-Cost Recovery in Real-Time Market
papers.abstract: We study ramping procurement co-optimized with economic dispatch under net-demand uncertainty. We examine two flexible ramp product designs implemented by grid operators: single-interval and multi-interval co-optimization. Both rely on rolling-window stochastic optimization with binding and advisory interval decisions. We develop analytical frameworks to evaluate generator profits, consumer payments, bid cost recovery (BCR), and operational efficiency. In particular, net-demand uncertainty may lead to generator under-compensation, requiring discriminatory BCR. While operational efficiency is invariant to energy and ramp prices, producer profits and consumer payments depend critically on pricing. We examine locational marginal pricing (LMP) and two uniform pricing: maximum dispatch cost pricing (MDCP) and maximum temporal locational marginal pricing (MTLMP). With out-of-market BCR, LMP yields discriminatory energy prices, whereas MDCP eliminates BCR and MTLMP does so in most cases. This property enables us to establish truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators under MDCP. Our analysis highlights trade-offs between single- and multi-interval co-optimization and pricing designs: multi-interval energy-ramp co-optimization outperforms single-interval co-optimization when ramping forecasts are accurate and ramping needs are tight, but its advantage diminishes under large forecast errors and moderate ramping needs. Empirical results on CAISO and ERCOT data show that MDCP and MTLMP increase producer profits with negligible BCR, albeit at the expense of higher consumer payments relative to LMP.

papers.title: Cooling, conduction, and compact objects: Gravothermal evolution of dissipative self-interacting dark matter halos
papers.abstract: Many proposed self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models yield radiative processes that can dissipate energy. Understanding their impact on astrophysical objects through simulations and comparing the results with observations may thus constrain SIDM models. We systematically investigated how dissipation alters the gravothermal evolution of isolated SIDM halos by independently varying dissipation and heat conduction and identified potential observational signatures. We present the first extension of the $N$-body formalism for frequent small-angle self-interactions to include effective dissipation. We compared all results for isolated halos with a dissipative gravothermal fluid model to assess the validity and limitations of the latter. We find that dissipation qualitatively changes the gravothermal evolution of SIDM halos beyond simply accelerating collapse. Sufficiently strong central cooling can invert the usual role of heat conduction: the formation of an isothermal core is suppressed such that conduction remains directed inward throughout the evolution. Outer halo regions beyond the scale radius can cool efficiently rather than being heated by conduction, resulting in a larger region of mass infall and a less pronounced indentation between the core and the outer halo in the final density profile. These effects depend strongly on the cooling rate but are comparatively insensitive to the angular dependence of the self-interaction cross section. We further show that weakly dissipative self-interactions can explain the properties of the recently observed strong lens perturber in JVAS B1938+666 with significantly shorter evolution times or, equivalently, smaller cross sections compared to the elastic case. Our results open a new route to connecting halo structure and recently reported compact objects to dark-sector microphysics.

papers.title: Global existence, blow-up behavior and numerical simulations for a class of chemotaxis-driven fish-mussel systems
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate a chemotaxis-driven fish--mussel ecosystem model described by a coupled system of partial differential equations subject to homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. Under suitable assumptions on the system parameters and initial data, we establish the global existence of classical solutions by employing semigroup methods together with a priori estimates. We also examine the possible blow-up behavior of solutions in a three-dimensional domain. To support the theoretical analysis, a finite element method is developed for the numerical approximation of the system, and convergence studies based on mesh refinement are carried out to verify the accuracy and stability of the proposed numerical scheme. Furthermore, numerical simulations illustrating the blow-up behavior of solutions in the computational domain are presented.

papers.title: Broadband High-Level Squeezed Light using Waveguide Optical Parametric Amplifiers with External Dispersion Compensation
papers.abstract: We demonstrate broadband phase-sensitive amplification (PSA) measurement of squeezed light generated by a waveguide optical parametric amplifier (OPA) with external dispersion compensation. In broadband systems, group velocity dispersion (GVD) induces a frequency-dependent rotation of the squeezing axis, which limits the observable bandwidth in PSA measurements. While dispersion compensation between two OPAs has been demonstrated previously, we show that the quantity to be compensated is not the material group-delay dispersion $D$ itself but a gain-dependent effective value $D\tanh r/(2r)$, where $r$ is the squeezing parameter, and realize the compensation with free-space fused-silica plates whose insertion loss is $0.4\%$. As a result, we observe a maximum squeezing of $5.9\pm0.2$~dB near the carrier frequency and more than 5~dB of squeezing up to a frequency offset of $5.9\pm0.1$ THz from the carrier. Furthermore, squeezing below the shot-noise level is confirmed up to a frequency offset of $6.9\pm0.1$ THz from the carrier, corresponding to the accessible phase-matching bandwidth of the waveguide OPA. Our results establish a practical method for broadband characterization of squeezed light and provide a key step toward ultrafast continuous-variable quantum information processing.

papers.title: Hybrid Analog-Digital Approximate Inverse Preconditioning for Krylov Methods
papers.abstract: Analog in-memory computing enables highly parallel matrix-vector multiplications with reduced data movement, but the resulting operations are noisy, quantized, and affected by device- and circuit-level non-idealities. This paper studies approximate inverse preconditioning for Krylov subspace methods in a hybrid analog-digital architecture that combines a conventional digital processor with an analog in-memory computing (AIMC) unit. The digital host performs sparse products with the coefficient matrix and the precision-sensitive Krylov operations, while the AIMC unit performs preconditioner applications through analog crossbar matrix-vector multiplications. Since the realized preconditioner is inexact and application-dependent, the outer iteration is formulated as the flexible GMRES method. We show that analog execution changes the usual preconditioner design problem in the sense that a stronger digital preconditioner may be less effective after analog scaling, write noise, input/output perturbations, quantization, and clipping are taken into account. We use exact block inverses and sparse approximate inverses as reference constructions and develop a noise-matching criterion for Monte Carlo approximate inverse (MCAI) construction. We also study damping and nesting to improve robustness. Numerical experiments, in which analog matrix-vector products are simulated rather than executed on hardware, show that analog-aware choices of block size, damping, MCAI construction accuracy, and nesting are important for robust convergence.

papers.title: Transverse Modulation of Continuous Electron Beams by a Structured Optical Cavity
papers.abstract: Compact aberration correction at large semi-angles remains a central challenge in electron microscopy. Here we propose a phase plate for continuous electron beams based on the ponderomotive interaction with an intracavity standing wave in a near-concentric Fabry--Pérot resonator. For electrons propagating along the cavity axis, a standing-wave with Laguerre-Gaussian mode of topological charge $l=1$ imprints an annular phase shift that is opposite in sign to the third-order spherical aberration of a conventional electron lens. For a \(5~\mathrm{keV}\) beam with a convergence semi-angle of \(25~\mathrm{mrad}\), we fully compensate the third-order spherical aberration of an objective lens with \(C_\mathrm{s}=1~\mathrm{mm}\), yielding the transverse width of the corrected probe in the focus of \(σ_\mathrm{p}=1.4~\mathrmÅ\). The accessible transverse electron phases are set by the supported resonator modal basis and its coherent superpositions.

papers.title: Mapping Domain-Wall Bayesian Reconstruction with LISA
papers.abstract: We study the Bayesian reconstruction of peaked domain-wall gravitational-wave signals with LISA and construct reconstruction maps over the signal-parameter plane. These maps identify regions where the signal can be probed with minimal posterior uncertainty and parameter degeneracy. Our analysis employs a two-parameter domain-wall spectral template and includes astrophysical foregrounds from Galactic double-white-dwarf binaries and extragalactic compact binaries, together with LISA instrumental noise. Bayesian inference is performed for 64 injections using nested sampling, and the resulting posterior quantities are interpolated with the Clough--Tocher method to generate smooth maps across parameter space. Under the adopted instrumental-noise and foreground assumptions, we find that LISA reconstructs domain-wall signals most effectively for annihilation temperatures $T_*\sim10^3\!-\!10^6\,\mathrm{GeV}$. In this regime, posteriors become tighter and less degenerate, enabling reliable two-parameter reconstruction. The most favorable region corresponds to signals with ${\rm SNR}\gtrsim50$, while signals with ${\rm SNR}\sim10$ remain reconstructable near $T_*\sim10^{5-6}\,\mathrm{GeV}$. This weaker-signal region corresponds approximately to $4\times10^{-12}\lesssimΩ_{\rm GW}^{\rm peak}h^2\lesssim4\times10^{-11}$ and $30\,\mathrm{mHz}\lesssim f_p\lesssim100\,\mathrm{mHz}$. Our results provide a quantitative reconstruction forecast for peaked domain-wall signals in the LISA band and a guide for particle-physics models predicting milli-Hz gravitational-wave spectra.

papers.title: Probabilistic Signature Inversion: Learning Conditional Distributions from Truncated Signatures
papers.abstract: The signature transform is a principled feature map for continuous-time paths, valued for its uniqueness and universality. Recovering a path from its truncated signature is, however, structurally ill-posed, because the truncated signature map is not injective. We therefore reframe truncated signature inversion as a probabilistic problem---learning the conditional distribution of a path given its truncated signature---and adopt a signature-conditioned flow matching model as a practical estimator. This formulation elucidates the fundamental difficulty of inversion: posterior-sampling reconstruction error quantifies the irreducible uncertainty remaining after conditioning on a statistic. For Gaussian process families, we derive this error from the tractable posterior under linear-statistics conditioning, obtaining a closed form for log-GBM and numerically tractable formulas for drifted fBM and OU. This oracle error upper-bounds the corresponding error under truncated-signature conditioning, since truncated signatures are more informative than linear statistics. The experimental results are consistent with the theoretical analysis: the learned sampler under linear-statistics conditioning closely matches the theoretically derived posterior in both reconstruction error and distribution, while reconstruction errors decrease under richer truncated-signature conditioning. Moreover, generated paths faithfully recover the conditioning signature and preserve key distributional and temporal structures. Together, these results establish a well-posed probabilistic framework for truncated-signature inversion, with applicability demonstrated on financial data beyond the process families covered by theory. Code is available at https://github.com/Junoh-Kang/ProbSigInv.

papers.title: Modeling inhomogeneous spatial point configurations with applications to replicated patterns in real-life waiting crowds
papers.abstract: In this article, we connect statistical inference for spatial point processes with the analysis of waiting pedestrian crowds through two interconnected contributions. First, on the methodological side we develop an inference procedure for semiparametric spatial point process models leveraging replicated spatial patterns, i.e., multiple approximately independent realizations from the same process. Second, we show that spatial point processes provide a suitable modeling framework for waiting pedestrians, capturing two key aspects: spatial inhomogeneity driven by location attractiveness and repulsive interactions between pedestrians. These two components are central to the inference problem itself, since spatial point process modeling hinges on disentangling background intensity from interaction. Although replicated spatial patterns are rare in point process literature, they are available here through a unique real-life pedestrian dataset, thereby directly linking the methodological development to the physical application. We use the proposed methods to fit and evaluate determinantal and Gibbs point processes in a simulation study and a real-world case study. Despite persistent challenges in decoupling the influences of inhomogeneity from interaction, these models are able to reproduce key empirical features of waiting pedestrians.

papers.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
papers.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8σ$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5σ$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.

papers.title: Ultrashort Two-Pulse Train Generation on a 100 TW Laser Beamline Using a Delay Mask After the Final Focusing Optics
papers.abstract: Experimental results showing the generation of an ultrashort two-pulse train using a two-section delay mask placed downstream of the off-axis parabola focusing optics are reported. Based on the initial simulation results, a circular fused silica plate with a central aperture and a measured thickness of $570\pm50$ $μ$m used in the quantitative delay calculation was designed to enable two distinct transverse portions of the incident laser pulse to be focused, ideally, with equal intensity. This fulfills one of the requirements of the resonant multi-pulse ionization injection (ReMPI) scheme for laser wakefield acceleration. As an intermediary step, a calibration of Gafchromic EBT4 films against laser fluence was established, enabling direct characterization of the unattenuated transverse beam profile. The experiment was carried out at the CNR-INO Intense Laser Irradiation Laboratory (ILIL) using a 240 TW laser system operated at 100 TW as part of the ongoing preparation for the first experimental demonstration of ReMPI. The pulse-to-pulse delay introduced by the delay mask was experimentally measured (at a reduced power, as customary for temporal autocorrelation measurements) to be $\simeq 901$ fs, in good agreement with the expected value of $\simeq 888$ fs. While the pulse-to-pulse delay is not yet optimized for ReMPI operation at practically relevant plasma densities, the experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed delay-mask concept.

papers.title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) -- Bayesian 3D shape inference of star-forming galaxy populations
papers.abstract: Understanding the intrinsic 3D shapes of galaxies provides crucial insights into their formation and evolution, but determining these from projections remains challenging. We apply a Bayesian inference framework to optical images of galaxies from the Euclid Data Release 1, leveraging its large sample size to test the scalability and robustness of this methodology. Applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to Sérsic axis ratios and effective radii, we constrain the population-level mean 3D ellipticity, triaxiality, and size, together with their covariances for $40\,864\,304$ star-forming galaxies with stellar masses $M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{10.5}M_\odot$ at redshifts $0<z<1.2$. Our sample size exceeds previous shape inference studies by factors of $440$--$52\,800$ relative to early observations by JWST, and factors of $440$--$17\,600$ relative to legacy observations from HST in overlapping mass-redshift bins, enabling finer binning alongside improved statistical constraints on shape evolution. We additionally include over 9 million galaxies at $z<0.5$, a regime historically limited by sample size in previous shape inference studies. We recover key evolutionary trends identified in previous smaller-sample studies. We find high ellipticities ($μ_E \sim 0.600$--$0.821$) across all bins, indicating that the underlying 3D shape distributions are statistically dominated by flattened geometries. Most notably, we recover the decline of the prolate fraction towards $z=0$ at low masses ($M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{9.5}M_\odot$) reported by previous studies. This trend is seen consistently in comparable analyses of independent data sets spanning different depths and resolution regimes, showing that it is not an artefact of small-sample statistics, suggesting it may be a genuine feature of galaxy evolution. We also identify future methodological improvements for subsequent Euclid data releases.

papers.title: From life-history model to theories of ecological diversity: the impact of Madhav Gadgil's work
papers.abstract: In this article, we review and provide perspectives on the foundational contributions of the renowned ecologist Madhav Gadgil, including the Gadgil-Bossert life-history model, ecological diversity, population biology, harvesting theory, human-ecological systems, co-evolution, adaptive management, and environmental democracy. We take the Gadgil-Bossert model of reproductive allocation as a starting point for reviewing Gadgil's broader contributions to evolutionary and population theory. Then we examine how density regulation shapes selection on reproductive allocation in his work on $r$- and $K$-selection. We then consider how interactions among genotypes determine whether a mixture can remain stable and resist invasion. We outline the key theoretical developments arising from these works and discuss their continued influence on contemporary ecological thought and present-day ecological systems.

papers.title: GV-subschemes and hyperelliptic Jacobians
papers.abstract: We provide a solution to the hyperelliptic Schottky problem: a principally polarized complex abelian variety whose theta divisor has singular locus of codimension three is a hyperelliptic Jacobian. As a key step towards this criterion for hyperelliptic Jacobians, we prove a conjecture of Pareschi and Popa which predicts that if the ideal sheaf $I_X$ of a subscheme $X$ of an indecomposable PPAV $(A, Θ)$ satisfies that $I_X(2Θ)$ is IT$_0$, then $X$ is a GV-subscheme. As a corollary of the main result, the base scheme of an ample line bundle on a complex abelian variety is generically reduced along every irreducible component of codimension $2$, confirming a conjecture of Debarre. This corollary completes the algebro-geometry proof by Arbarello-Codogni-Pareschi in \cite{ACP21, ACP25} of Novikov's conjecture, which characterizes Jacobians via the KP equation.

papers.title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
papers.abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.

papers.title: Radiation Hardness Assurance of Optical Coatings for the COMPASSO Iodine Reference
papers.abstract: The COMPASSO payload demonstrates compact iodine-based optical frequency references on the International Space Station (ISS), requiring optical windows and antireflective coatings that remain stable in the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) radiation environment. Radiation analysis was performed to quantify how trapped electrons, protons, and ions affect the fused-silica iodine cell and its coatings under mission-relevant shielding and exposure scenarios. The aim was to determine whether selected coatings meet the COMPASSO optical requirements after realistic LEO irradiation, identify degradation mechanisms linked to deposition technology and materials, and provide selection and qualification guidance for coatings in spaceborne iodine spectroscopy and precision optical-clock payloads. Nominal and worst-case electron, proton, and heavy-ion flux and fluence spectra for the ISS orbit were derived using the AE8/AP8, CREME96, ESP, and ISO15390 models. The ion component was assessed by simulation only, while irradiation tests used electrons and protons. Eight coating stacks produced by different deposition methods were exposed to proton and electron irradiation corresponding to nominal and worst-case mission loads. Pre- and post-irradiation characterization included reflectance and transmittance measurements, together with visual and microscopic inspection of coating integrity. These tests led to the selection of a four-layer Ta$_2$O$_5$/SiO$_2$ stack, which was used to produce the iodine cell optical window.
